name: Xeesal

card.summary: Xeesal is a cosmetic skin-lightening product used in sub-Saharan Africa to even out and lighten skin tone.
card.note: Skin-lightening products of this type have been linked in dermatology literature to adverse skin reactions.

quick.overview:
Xeesal is the name of a cosmetic skin-lightening product documented in a 2010 dermatology letter on cosmetic skin whitening in sub-Saharan Africa. People using products of this kind aim for a lighter or more even complexion.

Published information about the brand itself is limited to that report, which discusses it as one example within the wider practice of cosmetic skin lightening.
quick.how: Skin-lightening products are generally applied topically to the face and body as creams, lotions or soaps over an extended period. Specific routines for this brand are not described in the sources.
quick.risks: Dermatology literature on cosmetic skin lightening in Africa describes adverse reactions to lightening products, with the type of reaction depending on the active ingredients, which vary by product.

lead: Xeesal is a cosmetic skin-lightening product that appears in dermatology literature on skin whitening in sub-Saharan Africa. Skin lightening is practised by people who want a paler or more even complexion, and Xeesal is discussed as a named example of the products available in that market.[1]

The one source specific to the product is a 2010 letter in Actas Dermo-Sifiliograficas titled "Xeesal: Cosmetic skin whitening in subsaharan Africa".[1] Detailed information on its composition, manufacturer and use is limited.

chain: Applied topically as a lightening cosmetic
Reduces visible pigmentation over repeated use
angle.text: Users of skin-lightening cosmetics apply them with the aim of a lighter or more uniform complexion. Xeesal is described in a dermatology letter as one such product in sub-Saharan Africa.[1]

paras: Xeesal belongs to the category of cosmetic skin-whitening products reported in sub-Saharan Africa, where such products are sold for evening or lightening skin colour.[1]
Dermatologists writing on the topic discuss cosmetic skin lightening as a widespread practice with associated skin-health concerns, and the 2010 letter places Xeesal within that discussion.[1]
No studies found. The only published report is a descriptive letter on cosmetic skin whitening that names the product.[1]

timeline.event: Letter on Xeesal and cosmetic skin whitening in sub-Saharan Africa published.[1]
